themes.theme: Commission guidance on scope, prohibition and risk classification
themes.definition: Official Commission guidelines, interpretations and worked examples that help authorities, providers and deployers decide whether a tool is an AI system at all, whether it is a prohibited practice, whether it is high-risk, and what obligations follow.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act obliges the Commission to issue guidelines on the practical implementation of the Act, including on the prohibited practices in Article 5 and on how to apply the definition of an 'AI system' (EU046, Art. 96(1)(b) and (f)), and, after consulting the Board and no later than 2 February 2026, guidelines on the high-risk classification rule in Article 6 with practical examples of use cases that are and are not high-risk (Art. 6(5); Recital 53 says the same with 'should'). The Commission's later guidelines appear as the delivered resource: the prohibited-practices guidelines (EU043) present the separate definition guidelines as 'the Commission's interpretation' and promise further support to operators and authorities and more practical use cases 'on an ongoing basis', and the Article 50 transparency guidelines (EU_Art50) say they aim to assist competent authorities, providers and deployers in ensuring compliance, and point back to the definition guidelines in a footnote. What is provided is interpretation, not a decision: the classification is still made by whoever must apply the rules to a particular tool, and checked by the supervising authorities [inference]. Strength differs by document: the Act's articles use 'shall', the recital 'should', and the guidelines describe their 'aim' or what the Commission 'will' do, with nothing said about what happens if guidance is late or missing. The guidance documents cite one another rather than restating content, so a public body deciding whether its tool is in scope must assemble the answer from several Commission texts [inference].
themes.holders: The Commission (after consulting the Board, for the Article 6 guidelines). Named users: competent authorities, providers and deployers (EU_Art50); 'operators and authorities' (EU043).
themes.binding: Statutory duty on the Commission to produce guidelines (Art. 6(5) and Art. 96(1), 'shall'), with one dated deadline (2 February 2026); Recital 53 'should'; the guidelines themselves are non-binding interpretation ('the Commission's interpretation') and the ongoing-support commitment is a 'will'. If not met: not stated.
themes.checks: n/a (supports classifying a tool, not checking a tool or its outputs)

The Guidelines on the Definition of an AI system provide the Commission’s interpretation of that definition.
The Commission will provide additional support to operators and authorities how to understand the prohibitions and collect further practical use cases on an ongoing basis
these Commission Guidelines are issued with the aim to serve as practical guidance to assist competent authorities , as well as providers and deployers of AI systems, in ensuring compliance

themes.theme: Expert and advisory input to EU-level decisions
themes.definition: Advisory bodies, expert panels and methods that the AI Act and related guidelines provide to inform decisions taken by the Commission or the AI Office, especially on classifying systems and general-purpose models and on changing the Act's lists.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act surrounds Commission and AI Office decisions with several sources of advice: the Board 'may' issue recommendations and written opinions on any matter of implementation, on request or on its own initiative (Art. 66(e)); an advisory forum 'shall be established' to provide technical expertise to the Board and the Commission, with membership balanced between commercial and non-commercial interests (Art. 67(1), per the coder note); and a scientific panel of independent experts advises on classifying general-purpose AI models with systemic risk (Art. 68(3)(a)(iii)). The guidelines in EU088 mention a further pool of experts set up by the Joint Research Centre to advise the AI Office on categorising AI models. For changes to the Act's own lists (the Annex III high-risk uses, the Article 5 prohibitions and the Article 50 transparency cases, per the note), the AI Office must 'undertake to develop' an 'objective and participative methodology' for evaluating risk levels (Art. 112(11)). The omnibus amendment (EU_Omnibus) strengthens one channel: when assessing whether adherence to codes of practice is adequate, the Commission must take 'utmost account' of the Board's opinion. Throughout, advisers inform and the Commission or AI Office decides; the 'utmost account' wording is the only place in these passages that constrains how advice is used, and the forum's mixed membership means that official advice can include industry voices [inference].
themes.holders: European Artificial Intelligence Board; advisory forum; scientific panel of independent experts; the JRC pool of experts; the AI Office (methodology). The Commission and the AI Office are the decision-makers receiving the advice.
themes.binding: Statutory: the forum 'shall be established'; the AI Office 'shall undertake to develop' the methodology; the Board 'may' advise (a power, not a duty); under the omnibus text the Commission 'shall assess', taking 'utmost account' of the Board's opinion. The JRC pool is described, not mandated, in the passage. If not met: not stated.
themes.checks: Not a check on a tool's outputs. The one method here (EU-DM-RES-005) evaluates the risk levels of categories of systems: trigger: the possible inclusion of new systems in the Act's lists; compared against: 'the criteria outlined in the relevant Articles'; metric or threshold: not stated; who: the AI Office develops the method; result: feeds Commission decisions on amending Annex III, Article 5 and Article 50 (per the coder note). For the classification advice on general-purpose models (EU-DM-RES-016, -040): trigger, criteria and thresholds not stated in these passages.

quotes.quote: the AI Office shall undertake to develop an objective and participative methodology for the evaluation of risk levels based on the criteria outlined in the relevant Articles and the inclusion of new systems
providing advice on the classification of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk
the pool of experts , put into place by the Commission’s J oint Research Centre (‘JRC’) to provide the AI Office with advice on the categorisation of AI models

themes.theme: Means, competence and authority for the human overseer to intervene or stop
themes.definition: The built-in tools, guidance mechanisms and personal competence, training and authority that let a person assigned to oversee a high-risk AI system decide to intervene in it or stop it.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act places a duty on the provider, as appropriate and proportionate, to enable the person overseeing a high-risk system 'to intervene in the operation' of it or interrupt it through a 'stop' button or similar procedure that brings it to a halt in a safe state (EU046, Art. 14(4)(e)). Recital 73 adds that oversight measures should include 'mechanisms to guide and inform' the overseer in deciding 'if, when and how to intervene', and that overseers should have the necessary competence, training and authority; the Commission's prohibited-practices guidelines (EU043, para 204) restate the competence point with 'must'. The passive wording leaves the holder of each element unclear: the coder notes treat the stop mechanism and guidance mechanisms as the provider's to build, while assigning competent, trained people with authority would fall to whoever operates the system, the deployer [inference]. 'Authority' is itself a decision power rather than a resource, which is why the two coders split these passages between this cell and Decision-making/Design or Delivery/Resources. Nothing here says what information the guiding mechanisms must give, how the overseer should judge that the system is not performing as intended, or which outputs or cases must reach the overseer at all.
themes.holders: Not stated (passive wording). Nearest: providers (build the means to intervene and stop); the natural persons to whom human oversight is assigned (use them); deployers as the party assigning overseers [inference].
themes.binding: Art. 14(4)(e) is a statutory duty on the provider to enable intervention 'as appropriate and proportionate'; the coder note links breach to penalties under Art. 99(4)(a) via the provider obligations in Art. 16(a), outside this passage. Recital 73 is non-binding ('should'). EU043 restates the competence, training and authority requirement as a statutory duty ('must'), per the coding, without naming the article in the passage. If not met: otherwise not stated.
themes.checks: Trigger: during operation, whenever the overseer judges intervention necessary 'to avoid negative consequences or risks' (Recital 73; the coder note adds 'if it does not perform as intended'). Compared against: not stated. Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: the natural person assigned human oversight, using means built in by the provider. What happens with the result: the overseer may intervene, interrupt or stop the system so that it halts in a safe state; nothing on recording, reporting or reviewing the intervention.

quotes.quote: to intervene in the operation of the high-risk AI system or interrupt the system through a ‘stop’ button or a similar procedure that allows the system to come to a halt in a safe state

mechanisms to guide and inform a natural person to whom human oversight has been assigned to make informed decisions if, when and how to intervene in order to avoid negative consequences or risks, or stop the system
the human oversight must be assigned to persons with the necessary competence, training and authority

themes.theme: Information supplied to whoever decides on using a tool
themes.definition: Information that providers, Member State rules or code signatories must give to a deployer, a test participant or an authorising authority so that it can decide whether, and how, a particular tool is used.
themes.what_is_set_out: Four passages make information the resource for a specific decision on use. Under the AI Act, transparency and instructions for use should put deployers 'in a better position to make the correct choice' of system in light of their own obligations (EU046, Recital 72). Before high-risk systems are tested in real-world conditions, deployers or prospective deployers must be informed of all aspects of the testing relevant to their decision to take part and given the instructions for use, and testing may not go ahead otherwise (Art. 60(4)(h)). For real-time remote biometric identification, the Commission's prohibited-practices guidelines (EU043, para 416) say the Member State rules on requests should give the authorising authority 'relevant and complete information' so that it can decide on strict necessity and proportionality. In a code of practice whose signatories provide generative AI systems (EU121), deployers and other users are promised access to the providers' logging policies, but only where a provider uses the optional logging (per the coder note). The four differ sharply in strength: a statutory condition with a consequence (no testing), a recital, the Commission's reading of what national rules must contain, and a voluntary commitment by signatories.
themes.holders: Providers or prospective providers (instructions for use; test information); Member States (rules for authorisation requests) with the requesting deployer supplying the information; signatories who provide generative AI systems (logging policies). Recipients: deployers, prospective deployers, other users, the authorising authority.
themes.binding: Art. 60(4)(h) is a statutory condition: if not met, testing may not be conducted. Recital 72 is non-binding. EU043 restates a statutory duty on Member States to set rules; consequence not stated. EU121 is a voluntary commitment by signatories ('will be given'), applying only where optional logging is used.
themes.checks: For the real-time biometric identification authorisation (EU-DM-RES-017): trigger: before use, on a request; compared against: strict necessity and proportionality; metric or threshold: not stated; who: the authorising authority; what happens with the result: it decides whether to authorise the use (the coder note adds that logging is made available to the authority). For real-world testing (EU-DM-RES-013): the passage covers information for the decision to take part, not the test itself; test criteria not stated here. No check on outputs.

quotes.quote: the latter have been informed of all aspects of the testing that are relevant to their decision to participate, and given the relevant instructions for use of the AI system referred to in Article 13

which are aimed at providing relevant and complete information as to the use of real-time RBI systems to the authorising authority to enable it to decide as to the strict necessity and proportionality of such use.
Deployers and other users of the generative AI systems will be given access to the logging policies
Deployers should, inter alia, be in a better position to make the correct choice of the system that they intend to use in light of the obligations applicable to them

themes.theme: Staff, expertise and training for the bodies that decide
themes.definition: Requirements or recommendations that bodies taking decisions about AI have enough competent people, in-house AI expertise, the right members, or training in applying the rules.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act requires notifying authorities, whose task the coder note links to designation decisions under Art. 28(1) (designating the bodies that carry out conformity assessments [inference]), to have 'an adequate number of competent personnel', with expertise in fields such as information technology, AI and law, including the supervision of fundamental rights (EU046, Art. 28(7)). The European Parliament document (EP2024) proposes that AI profiles such as data scientists, AI architects and engineers 'must be recruited' so that the administration has the knowledge, control and oversight of AI technologies, and that its Governance Board 'shall include' the ICT services and key representatives of the administration (which representatives is not stated). The JRC handbook (JRC129100) is hedged: even in countries whose AI strategy is led by the private sector, the public sector 'may still be very much required' to keep enough internal capacity and expertise to spot where AI could help, and it suggests context-related training modules, for example to support applying EU regulations in national and local law. Strength therefore runs from a statutory 'shall' on a regulatory authority, through a proposed internal rule for one institution, to suggestions in a research handbook. None of these passages sets numbers, budgets or skill standards beyond 'adequate' or 'the right level'.
themes.holders: Notifying authorities; Parliament's administration (nearest named actor, passive wording) and its Governance Board; 'the public sector' in countries with private sector-led strategies (JRC handbook); training provider not stated.
themes.binding: Art. 28(7) is a statutory 'shall'; if not met: not stated. EP2024 uses 'must' and 'shall' in a proposed internal framework; if not met: not stated. JRC129100 recommends or suggests, with hedged wording; if not met: not stated.

quotes.quote: Notifying authorities shall have an adequate number of competent personnel at their disposal for the proper performance of their tasks.

Specific AI-related profiles, such as data scientists, AI architects and engineers must be recruited to ensure that the administration possesses the right level of knowledge, control and oversight of the AI technologies.
ensure that enough internal capacity and expertise on AI is present t o detect opportunities where AI may improve work relations

themes.theme: Adoption frameworks and use-case lists for public administrations
themes.definition: Frameworks, use-case lists, readiness guidance and awareness-raising, from the Joint Research Centre, offered to governments and public administrations to inform decisions on whether and where to adopt AI and on national strategy.
themes.what_is_set_out: The two JRC reports present themselves as resources for adoption decisions. The handbook (JRC129100) says its recommendations 'can serve to assess their AI readiness' and foster implementation, and calls for awareness among politicians and governments of the value of investing in data infrastructures (a passage the coder flagged as being about open data generally). The later report (JRC143539) identifies application fields and use cases (three fields and 13 use cases, per the note) where AI shows 'significant potential for public value creation', to support prioritisation; it invites administrations to run similar evaluations to customise the list, and offers its adoption framework (anchor, adapt, apply, with assessment and monitoring, per the note) as 'an operational reference' for national strategies. These lists point in the opposite direction from the AI Act's lists of high-risk use cases: they are offered to find places to adopt AI, not to restrict it. Everything here is offered or recommended, not required, and no one is obliged to use it.
themes.holders: JRC report and handbook authors (provide). Intended users: policymakers, practitioners and stakeholders, public administrations, Member States designing national strategies, and politicians and governments (the target of awareness-raising; the actor raising awareness is not stated).
themes.binding: Not binding: offered ('can serve') or recommended ('there is a need'). If not met: not stated.
themes.checks: n/a (the JRC adoption framework includes assessment and monitoring, per the coder note, but these passages give no trigger, comparison, metric or owner)

quotes.quote: To support this prioritisation, this report identifies key AI application fields (11) and use cases (12) where AI shows significant potential for public value creation
The adoption framework presented in this report can serve as an operational reference also for the design of national strategies.
the recommendations and actions presented in this handbook can serve to assess their AI readiness and foster implementation in their public administrations.
there is a need to raise awareness amongst politicians and governments of the value and potential return on investment in data i nfrastructures

themes.theme: Risk and impact assessment tools for deciding on use
themes.definition: Methods and guidance that help an organisation or its staff judge the risks, limitations or expected impact of an AI tool before deciding whether or how to use it.
themes.what_is_set_out: The EDPS risk-management document (EDPS_AI_risk) supplies a concrete tool: risk evaluated as the product of likelihood and severity of impact, shown in a qualitative risk matrix with a five-level scale (per the coder note), serving EU institutions' decisions on how to evaluate and treat risks. The Commission's staff guidelines (EC_staff_GenAI_2023) are designed to help staff members 'assess the risks and limitations' of generative AI tools available online, explaining what generative AI is and naming example tools (per the note). The JRC handbook (JRC129100) says impact assessment frameworks 'need to be developed' to guide decision-makers and practitioners in introducing AI and in knowing what impact to expect: a gap identified, not a tool supplied. So one document provides a method, one gives orientation to individual staff, and one calls for frameworks that do not yet exist. None sets a level of risk or impact above which a tool should not be used.
themes.holders: EDPS (provides the matrix, for EU institutions); the European Commission as issuer of the staff guidelines (users: staff members); developer of impact assessment frameworks not stated (users: decision-makers and practitioners).
themes.binding: Provided guidance (EDPS; Commission staff guidelines) and a recommendation ('need to be developed', JRC). If not met: not stated.
themes.checks: Trigger: before use or introduction (staff assessing online tools; organisations introducing AI); for the EDPS matrix, as part of risk management, timing not stated in the passage. Compared against: likelihood and severity of impact (EDPS); expected impact (JRC); 'risks and limitations', otherwise unspecified (Commission staff guidelines). Metric or threshold: a qualitative five-level scale and likelihood-by-severity matrix (EDPS), with no acceptance threshold stated; not stated for the others. Who: EU institutions (EDPS); individual staff members (Commission); decision-makers and practitioners (JRC). What happens with the result: feeds the decision on treating the risk (EDPS, per the note); otherwise not stated. None of these checks the outputs of a tool in use: nothing on accuracy, consistency, prompts, model versions or confidence scores.

quotes.quote: the risk can be evaluated as the product of its likelihood and the severity of its impact (Risk = Likelihood x Impact). This is typically represented via a risk matrix (see Figure 2).
These guidelines are designed to help staff members (1) assess the risks and limitations of online available generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools

impact assessment frameworks need to be developed to guide decision -makers and practitioners to introduce AI in their own organisations, and identify what impact they should expect from their deployment

themes.theme: Facilitating voluntary codes of conduct and practice
themes.definition: Official encouragement and facilitation of voluntary codes through which providers and deployers set standards for AI systems beyond what the law requires, and the Commission's assessment of whether codes of practice are adequate.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act requires the AI Office and the Member States to 'encourage and facilitate' codes of conduct for applying the high-risk requirements voluntarily to other AI systems (EU046, Art. 95(1)), and to 'facilitate' codes for voluntarily applying specific requirements, including by deployers, to all AI systems (Art. 95(2)); per the coder note, such codes rest on clear objectives and key performance indicators and can cover Union ethical guidelines, environmental impact and AI literacy. The resource is facilitation: the authorities help others set standards rather than set them, and the passages do not say what facilitation consists of (money, staff, templates or meetings). The omnibus amendment (EU_Omnibus) concerns a separate instrument, codes of practice: replacing Art. 50(7), it has the Commission, taking utmost account of the Board's opinion, assess whether adherence to those codes is adequate. A public body acting as deployer could adopt a code of conduct, but nothing in these passages requires it to [inference].
themes.holders: AI Office and the Member States (encourage and facilitate); providers and deployers (voluntary drafters and adopters); the Commission, advised by the Board (adequacy of codes of practice).
themes.binding: Statutory duty to encourage and facilitate ('shall'); application by providers and deployers is voluntary; the Commission 'shall assess' adequacy under the omnibus text. If not met: not stated.
themes.checks: n/a (the Commission's adequacy assessment concerns codes, not tools or outputs; its criteria are not stated in the passage)

quotes.quote: The AI Office and the Member States shall encourage and facilitate the drawing up of codes of conduct, including related governance mechanisms, intended to foster the voluntary application to AI systems, other than high-risk AI systems
The AI Office and the Member States shall facilitate the drawing up of codes of conduct concerning the voluntary application, including by deployers, of specific requirements to all AI systems

themes.theme: Data-protection guidance pointed to for scope and role decisions
themes.definition: Existing guidance from data-protection bodies (the EDPB, the EDPS and the former Article 29 Working Party) that AI documents point readers to when they must decide how a data-protection concept applies to an AI tool.
themes.what_is_set_out: Three documents point to guidance they do not reproduce. The Commission's prohibited-practices guidelines (EU043) note that the EDPB has adopted guidelines on 'profiling', which matters for deciding whether a practice falls under the Article 5(1)(d) prohibition. The EDPS orientations on generative AI (EDPS_GenAI_orientations) advise EU institutions to follow the EDPS guidelines on controller, processor and joint controllership, which serves the decision on who holds which role for a generative AI system (per the coder note). EU074 tells supervisory authorities that they 'should consider' the Article 29 Working Party's Opinion 05/2014 on anonymisation techniques, serving their decision on whether data is anonymous (per the note). The strength is advisory throughout ('advised to follow', 'should consider', or a bare mention), and the resource is a pointer to older, general data-protection guidance rather than guidance written for AI tools [inference].
themes.holders: EDPB, EDPS and the Article 29 Working Party (authors of the guidance pointed to). Users: readers applying Article 5(1)(d); EU institutions (EUIs); supervisory authorities (SAs).
themes.binding: Advisory: 'advised to follow' (EDPS), 'should consider' (EU074), a mention (EU043). If not met: not stated.

themes.theme: Internal advice and inventories for institutions' own AI initiatives
themes.definition: Internal advisory committees, support groups and lists of initiatives that EU institutions set up to inform their own decisions on which AI initiatives to approve, invest in or prioritise.
themes.what_is_set_out: The Commission's AI@EC document (AIatEC) gives the ISG-AI the task of supporting the Information Technology and Cybersecurity Board (ITCB) 'in assessing new AI initiatives', and sets an operational action to establish and maintain a list of existing AI initiatives and propose their prioritisation for the creation of corporate AI services; the coder note says proposing is advisory and the decision sits with the ISG-AI and corporate IT governance. The European Court of Auditors (ECA_strategy) has an Advisory Committee on AI that advises 'on institutional compliance with the regulatory framework governing the use of AI', and commits to prioritise initiatives and allocate adequate resources where most needed. In both institutions the resource is advice and information, and the decision stays with a separate board or with the institution's management [inference for the ECA]. The passages do not say on what criteria initiatives are assessed or prioritised.
themes.holders: ISG-AI (supporting the ITCB); AI@EC Network, ISG-AI and corporate governance boards (list and prioritisation proposals); the ECA's Advisory Committee on AI; the European Court of Auditors (prioritisation and resource allocation).
themes.binding: Internal mandate with a timeline (AIatEC); an internal advisory role and a self-commitment ('crucial') at the ECA. Not statutory. If not met: not stated.
themes.checks: For assessing new AI initiatives (EU-DM-RES-043): trigger: a new AI initiative, before investment; compared against: not stated; metric or threshold: not stated; who: the ISG-AI in support of the ITCB; what happens with the result: not stated in the passage (the ITCB decides, per the coder note). Not a check on a tool's outputs.

quotes.quote: support the Information Technology and Cybersecurity Board in assessing new AI initia tives
Establish and maintain a list of existing AI initiatives and propose their prioritisation in view of the creation of corporate AI services.

quotes.location: AI governance at the ECA, para 17 (p. 7)
quotes.quote: advising on institutional compliance with the regulatory framework governing the use of AI

themes.theme: Unquantified calls for dedicated or adequate resources
themes.definition: Statements that decision-making on AI needs dedicated or adequate resources, without saying what kind, how much, or from whom.
themes.what_is_set_out: Two documents state the need for resources only in general terms. The JRC report (JRC143539) says that treating the public sector as a strategic domain 'requires clear governance arrangements, dedicated resources and well-defined responsibilities across levels of administration', in a recommendation addressed to Member States. The European Court of Auditors (ECA_strategy) calls it 'crucial' to prioritise initiatives and ensure that adequate resources are allocated where most needed. Neither passage names an amount, a budget line, a source of funds or the kind of resource meant. Together with the 'adequate number of competent personnel' required of notifying authorities (EU046, Art. 28(7), in the staffing theme), this is as close as the cell comes to money: no passage actually provides funding.
themes.holders: Member States (JRC recommendation); the European Court of Auditors (its own commitment).
themes.binding: A recommendation ('requires') and an institutional self-commitment ('crucial'). If not met: not stated.

quotes.quote: Recognising the public sector as a strategic domain requires clear governance arrangements, dedicated resources and well-defined responsibilities across levels of administration.
it is crucial to carefully prioritise initiatives and ensure that adequate resources are allocated where most needed.

absences: Decision-making starting codes: no passage provides resources for an authority's decision to approve, pause, restrict or withdraw a tool; resources for overriding outputs appear only as the general power to intervene in or stop a system (Art. 14(4)(e)), with nothing on disregarding or reversing a particular output; resources for appointing who decides appear only in the composition of the European Parliament's Governance Board; nothing supports issuing mandates. Resources starting codes: money is never quantified (only 'dedicated' or 'adequate' resources); time appears only as a deadline on the Commission (2 February 2026 for the Article 6 guidelines), never as time given to those who decide; data appears only as awareness of the value of investing in data infrastructure; access only as access to logging policies; there are no templates. Beyond the starting codes, a reader would expect but does not find: resources for national competent or market surveillance authorities to take decisions on tools, other than guidance said to assist them [inference: such provisions may be coded in other cells]; resources for a public body, as deployer, to decide whether to deploy, continue or stop a high-risk tool, beyond instructions for use and general frameworks; any criteria or information telling the human overseer when to intervene; and anything on checking outputs: accuracy, consistency or repeatability, prompts and configuration, model versions, confidence scores, or which cases reach a human.
cross_cutting: This cell is dominated by guidance and advice rather than people, money or tools: Commission guidelines that help actors decide whether a tool is an AI system, prohibited or high-risk; advisory bodies and expert panels feeding Commission and AI Office decisions; and JRC frameworks and use-case lists offered to administrations deciding where to adopt AI. Most of what is 'provided' is interpretation or advice that leaves the decision with someone else, and much of it is a pointer to another document rather than the resource itself. Binding force is uneven: the AI Act imposes 'shall' duties on the Commission, the AI Office, Member States and notifying authorities to produce guidance, methods, facilitation or staff, with no stated consequence if they fall short, while recitals, guidelines, JRC reports and institutions' internal documents use 'should', 'can serve', 'will' or 'must' without sanctions; the only stated consequence in the cell is that real-world testing may not go ahead unless deployers have been informed. Holders are overwhelmingly EU-level bodies (Commission, AI Office, Board, JRC, EDPS), while public bodies as deployers appear mainly as recipients of instructions, information and frameworks; the EU institutions' own documents (Parliament, Court of Auditors, Commission) add in-house expertise and advisory groups for their own AI decisions. Money is almost absent: 'dedicated' or 'adequate' resources are named but never quantified. On checking AI outputs, the cell offers only the overseer's means to intervene or stop a high-risk system and the competence, training and authority to do so; it says nothing about what outputs are compared against, about accuracy, consistency, prompts, model versions or confidence scores, or about which cases reach a human. Only 15 of the 45 passages were placed in this cell by both coders (18 by one coder only; 12 placed elsewhere by the other coder), so the boundary between this cell and Decision-making/Design, Delivery/Resources and Coordination/Design is soft.
